intervention: Town of Baldwin (population ~1,400) purchased and operated Baldwin Market, a municipally owned, town-payroll grocery store, after the town's previous private grocer closed in 2019.
outcome: Financial sustainability of a fully town-owned grocery store
finding: Baldwin Market opened in 2019 as a fully town-owned, town-payroll grocery store after the town's previous private grocer closed. Run not-for-profit, it operated at a loss for most of its life; as a single store it could not buy at wholesale prices, which made it hard to price groceries competitively. The town closed the store in March 2024, after about five years of operation.

source_title: Should Cities Open Their Own Grocery Stores?

transfer_note: Baldwin, FL is a town of ~1,400 people with a single-store retail market; Rock County's USDA-designated tracts hold 41,768 people in a small-metro area (Beloit/Janesville) with existing retail competition. Scale, financing options, and competitive context are not comparable, and Baldwin's specific failure mode (no wholesale purchasing power as a single tiny store) is partly a small-town problem a larger operation would not automatically share. It is nonetheless real-world evidence that public ownership alone did not guarantee viability in a documented case of the same ownership model (direct town-payroll operation, not a co-op or public-private partnership).

jurisdiction: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania (Hill District, compared to Homewood)
intervention: Opening of a new full-service supermarket (Shop 'n Save) in Pittsburgh's Hill District in October 2013 -- the neighborhood's first in about 30 years, following a public-led effort to attract a grocer -- studied against the similarly under-served Homewood neighborhood, which received no new store.

The only outcome tied to regular use of the new store was improved perceived access to healthy food, not measured diet or weight.

jurisdiction: Bronx, New York City (Morrisania, compared to Highbridge)
intervention: A new, government-subsidized (NYC FRESH program) full-service supermarket opened in the Morrisania section of the Bronx in August 2011 (about two months after the study's baseline survey concluded); studied against Highbridge, a comparable Bronx neighborhood that did not receive a new store, surveying caregivers of children ages 3-10.
outcome: Home food availability and children's dietary intake
finding: One year after the new supermarket opened, researchers found no appreciable difference in the availability of healthful or unhealthful foods at home, and no appreciable change in children's dietary intake, between the neighborhood that got the new store and the comparison neighborhood that did not.
effect_reported: No statistically significant difference-in-differences effect at 1 year (2,172 street-intercept surveys; 363 dietary recalls)

jurisdiction: United States (national, using Nielsen retail scanner and household panel data)
intervention: Not a single site intervention: a national quasi-experimental and structural-demand analysis using supermarket entries/exits and households moving between food environments as natural experiments, decomposing how much of the diet-quality gap between high- and low-income US households is explained by differential retail access ('supply') versus differences in what people choose to buy when access is held constant ('demand').
outcome: Nutritional inequality between high- and low-income US households
finding: Using new supermarket entries and household moves as natural experiments, the authors find that giving low-income households the same products and prices available to high-income households would close only about ten percent of the nutritional-inequality gap between rich and poor. The remaining roughly 90 percent is explained by differences in demand, not access. New store openings, on their own, are a small part of the story.
effect_reported: Equalizing food access is estimated to close only about 10% of the diet-quality gap between high- and low-income households; the remaining ~90% is attributed to demand-side factors
source_title: Food Deserts and the Causes of Nutritional Inequality
citation: Allcott, H., Diamond, R., Dube, J.-P., Handbury, J., Rahkovsky, I., & Schnell, M. (2019). Food deserts and the causes of nutritional inequality. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 134(4), 1793-1844. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjz015
transfer_note: This is the most methodologically rigorous study in this evidence set (natural-experiment identification plus a structural demand model on national retail-panel data), and it is also the strongest disconfirming evidence for a supply-side 'build a store, fix the diet' theory of change: it finds new store access explains a small share of the outcome the policy is implicitly trying to move. It is national in scope, not specific to Rock County or to a publicly owned store, but its conclusion -- that access is not the dominant constraint -- bears directly on what a Rock County store could and could not be expected to accomplish, regardless of ownership structure.

jurisdiction: Multiple (systematic review of studies published 1974-2018, primarily United States, Canada, and United Kingdom)
intervention: Systematic review of 80 retail food environment interventions (86 articles) -- new stores, store conversions, mobile markets, financing incentives, and related retail-access changes -- assessing their effect on diet and health, with a specific focus on the enabling role of public policy.
outcome: Diet and health outcomes across 80 distinct retail food environment interventions
finding: About 67% of the reviewed studies (58 of 86 articles) found at least one positive effect on diet, but 43% also reported null findings within the same body of evidence, and most studies used brief, purchasing-based measures rather than measured dietary intake (only 28%, or 24 articles, measured actual intake). Most interventions were framed around private retailers responding to consumers rather than public ownership, and 63% of studies (54 of 86 articles) did not discuss the enabling public policy at all -- the evidence base has little to say specifically about publicly-owned grocery models like AB1221's.
effect_reported: 58/86 articles (~67%) report >=1 positive diet effect; 43% also report null findings; 28% (24 articles) measured actual dietary intake; 63% (54 articles) did not discuss enabling policy
source_title: A Systematic Review of the Effect of Retail Food Environment Interventions on Diet and Health with a Focus on the Enabling Role of Public Policies
citation: Mah, C. L., Luongo, G., Hasdell, R., Taylor, N. G. A., & Lo, B. K. (2019). A systematic review of the effect of retail food environment interventions on diet and health with a focus on the enabling role of public policies. Current Nutrition Reports, 8(4), 411-428. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13668-019-00295-z (open-access full text: PMC6904419)
transfer_note: This is a synthesis across many jurisdictions and store types, not a Rock-County-specific or public-ownership-specific finding -- it establishes the general shape of the evidence base (mixed, measurement-limited, policy-context-thin) rather than a single transferable effect size. Its most load-bearing point for this page is negative: the literature it reviews barely engages with publicly owned retail as a distinct model, which is exactly AB1221's approach, so this review cannot confirm or rule out that specific model's effect.
